kurals.tamil:
இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு ஆயினும் ஊடுதல்
வல்லது அவர்அளிக்கு மாறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Illai thavaravarkku aayinum ootudhal
Valladhu avaralikku maaru.
kurals.meaning: Even when he has done nothing wrong, a little lovers’ sulking has the power to draw out more of his tenderness.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes two best friends pretend to be cross for a minute, just so the other one will come and make a fuss over them. Nobody did anything wrong; the little pout simply makes the kindness show. The wife in this poem says a small, pretend quarrel does the same for her husband’s love.
kurals.university: The final chapter of the Kural, ūṭal uvakai (‘the joy of lovers’ pique’), turns ūṭal, the feigned or playful sulking of a beloved, from a source of pain in the preceding chapters (pulavi, pulavi nuṇukkam) into a source of delight. Here the wife concedes illai tavaṟu avarkku (‘there is no fault in him’), yet ūṭutal (sulking) is vallatu (‘has the power’) to bring about avar aḷi (his tender grace, aḷi meaning lavish affection). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss the line as ūṭal making him shower greater love on her, and Kalaignar generalises it to lovers on both sides; Pope’s ‘fretful jealousy’ reads the pique more darkly than the Tamil commentators do. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; commentators traditionally assign the opening couplets of the chapter to the wife.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna playfully teases his devoted queen Rukmini by suggesting she would have done better to marry a worthier king; she is so stricken that she faints, and he at once lifts and consoles her, after which their affection is described as all the sweeter.
hinduism.explanation: The episode is the tradition’s classic lovers’ quarrel (praṇaya-kalaha) in which no real wrong has been done, yet the brief hurt brings out an outpouring of tenderness.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, the quarrel has no fault behind it, and its only result is a greater show of love.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; a genuine faultless love-quarrel that ends in deeper tenderness, though here the husband starts the teasing rather than the wife.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs, read in Christian tradition as a love poem and an allegory of divine love, joins love’s strength to the burning intensity of jealousy.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural, too, treats a flare of pique as part of love’s strength rather than a sign that love has failed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); it links love and jealous fire, but lacks the Kural’s point that a faultless partner is sulked at to draw out tenderness.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet told Aisha that he could tell when she was pleased with him and when she was cross: when pleased she swore by the Lord of Muhammad, and when cross by the Lord of Abraham. Aisha answered that even then she left out only his name, not her love for him.
islam.explanation: The hadith shows a loving marriage in which small displeasures are noticed, gently teased, and understood as love in disguise.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the wife’s little pique is affectionate rather than hostile, and her husband meets it with fond attention.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested hadith (page not re-read in this session, so not quoted); a close, tender parallel on affectionate sulking within marriage.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that any love which depends on some particular thing ends when that thing is gone, but love which depends on nothing never ends, giving David and Jonathan as its example.
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot distinguishes conditional love from love that needs no cause and therefore cannot be undone.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s couple has such a love: because nothing is wrong, the sulk cannot threaten it and only makes it show.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known mishnah; it speaks of love’s security in general, not of lovers’ quarrels, so it is a next-best match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells a householder that a husband should honour his wife by courtesy, by not despising her, by faithfulness, by handing over authority to her and by giving her adornments, and that she in turn shows him love in her own ways.
buddhism.explanation: The Sigalovada Sutta describes marriage as mutual, attentive regard on both sides.
buddhism.tie_back: The tenderness the Kural’s wife draws out by sulking is the kind of attentive regard the Buddha asks husbands to show.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (tr. Narada Thera; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a real Buddhist teaching on a husband’s attentiveness, but it has no idea of playful sulking, so this is a next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra teaches that anger destroys affection, pride destroys humility, deceit destroys friendship, and greed destroys everything.
jainism.explanation: Jain ethics treats anger (krodha) as one of the four passions (kaṣāya) and warns that it ruins love between people.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural claims the opposite for a playful, faultless sulk, which the Jain text would still count as a small stirring of passion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse; included as an honest contrast, since Jain teaching sees any anger as harmful to love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pausanias tells how Hera, angry with Zeus, withdrew from him to Euboea; Zeus, unable to win her back, dressed a wooden image as a bride and pretended to be marrying it. Hera rushed to the procession, tore off the veil, found the statue, laughed, and was reconciled to him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Boeotian Daedala festival remembered a divine lovers’ quarrel that ended in laughter and reunion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hera’s withdrawal, like the Kural’s sulk, serves to draw out a wooing that ends in renewed affection.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known aetiological myth; a close match on a quarrel that draws out wooing, though the reason for Hera’s anger is not given.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Terence’s comedy Andria, an old man remarks that the quarrels of lovers are the renewal of love (Latin: amantium irae amoris integratio est).
philosophy.explanation: The line became proverbial in Europe for the idea that a lovers’ quarrel freshens rather than ends their love.
philosophy.tie_back: It is almost a Latin restatement of this couplet’s claim that a faultless sulk draws out greater love.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one in idea; the Latin line is well attested, but it was not re-checked against a live text in this session, so it is given as paraphrase.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடலின் தோன்றும் சிறுதுனி நல்லளி
வாடினும் பாடு பெறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodalin thoandrum sirudhuni nallali
Vaatinum paadu perum.
kurals.meaning: The small pain that a lovers’ sulk brings may make his kindness droop for a while, but it will come back with greater glory.
kurals.elementary: A plant that is not watered for one day droops a little, and when you water it again it seems to stand up even taller. A short, small quarrel is like that: love looks a little wilted for a moment, then bounces back stronger.
kurals.university: The couplet sets ciṟu tuṉi (‘a small distress’, tuṉi meaning grief or estrangement) arising from ūṭal against nal aḷi (‘good tender love’), which may vāṭiṉum (‘even if it should wither’, a plant metaphor) yet pāṭu peṟum (‘will gain greatness’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take aḷi as the husband’s love that seems to fade during the sulk and then grows in worth; Puliyur Kesikan adds pinnar (‘afterwards’), making the gain explicitly temporal, and Pope renders the sense as feigned anger making drooping affection ‘bloom again’. Both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the same text; the botanical verb vāṭu (to wilt) is characteristic of the Kural’s Inbam imagery.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Rasa-lila of the Bhagavata Purana, when the gopis grow proud of Krishna’s attention he suddenly vanishes; they search the forest for him in anguish, and when he reappears their joy and his tenderness are greater than before.
hinduism.explanation: The tradition presents a brief separation within love as a way of deepening it.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a short spell in which love seems to wilt ends with that love shining more brightly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a real case of love lessened for a while and then renewed, though it is devotional and the separation is Krishna’s doing, not a wife’s sulk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows anger but sets it a short limit, so that it ends before it can harden.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s sulk is a short, harmless anger of exactly this kind, ending before it does damage.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); it shares the idea of brief, contained anger, but does not say that anger renews love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if a woman fears from her husband contempt or evasion, there is no sin upon them if they make terms of settlement between them - and settlement is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an encourages spouses to settle tensions between them, calling reconciliation the best course.
islam.tie_back: The Kural assumes the same arc: a passing distress between spouses resolved into something better than before.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih; quotation stops before the verse ends); it addresses real marital strain, not playful sulking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For His anger is but for a moment, His favour is for a life-time; weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist contrasts a brief anger with a lasting favour, and a night of tears with morning joy.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘small distress’ is just such a passing anger, after which love returns more glorious.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a strong match on brief anger giving way to joy, though it speaks of God, not lovers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world, but only by non-hatred, and calls this an eternal law.
buddhism.explanation: Hostility ends only when one side lets go of it rather than answering in kind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s sulk passes for the same reason: the husband answers it with tenderness, not anger.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous verse; it concerns real enmity rather than lovers’ play, so the fit is partial.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami tells Indra that anger and pride drag a person down rather than raising him.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural says the pain of a sulk will win glory, Jain teaching warns that anger and pride (the stuff of a sulk) lead downward.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; an honest contrast, since Jainism sees no gain in anger or pride.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I must go and see them that I may make peace between them; they have been quarrelling, and are so angry that they have not slept with one another this long while; if I can bring them round and restore them to one another’s embraces, they will be grateful to me and love me for ever afterwards.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hera pretends she is off to reconcile the primeval couple Oceanus and Tethys, whose quarrel has kept them apart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The image of an estranged couple restored to each other’s embraces is the Kural’s withered love made glorious again.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; the quarrel and reconciliation fit, though Hera’s tale is a ruse and the quarrel is not playful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: On his last day Socrates, rubbing his leg after the fetters are removed, remarks how strangely pleasure is related to pain: they never come to a man together, yet whoever pursues one is generally compelled to take the other, as if they were joined at a single head.
philosophy.explanation: Plato has Socrates notice that pain and pleasure follow close upon each other.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s small pain of sulking is followed, by the same linkage, by the pleasure of love regained.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a good philosophical match on pain giving way to pleasure, though not about love.

kurals.tamil:
புலத்தலின் புத்தேள்நாடு உண்டோ நிலத்தொடு
நீரியைந் தன்னார் அகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Pulaththalin puththelnaadu undoa nilaththodu
Neeriyainh thannaar akaththu.
kurals.meaning: With a lover whose heart is blended with mine like water with earth, is there any heaven that could match the joy of a little sulking?
kurals.elementary: When rain soaks into soil, you cannot pull the water back out; the two become one. When two people are that close, even a pretend grumble between them feels happy, because nothing can really pull them apart.
kurals.university: Pulattal (‘sulking’, a synonym of ūṭal) is weighed against puttēḷ nāṭu (‘the land of the gods’, heaven), and the rhetorical uṇṭō (‘is there?’) denies that heaven could be sweeter. The simile nilattoṭu nīr iyaintu aṉṉār (‘those who are like water joined with earth’) recalls the famous Kuṟuntokai 40 image of hearts mingled like red earth and rain (cempulap peyalnīr), signalling an inseparable union in which a quarrel holds no danger. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan all read the line as ‘is the gods’ world sweeter than sulking with such a lover?’, while Kalaignar renders puttēḷ nāṭu more freely as ‘a new world’. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh prints the sandhi form nīriyain tannār).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kalidasa opens the Raghuvamsha by saluting Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, as joined together like a word and its meaning.
hinduism.explanation: The image describes a divine couple so united that one cannot exist apart from the other.
hinduism.tie_back: Kalidasa’s word-and-meaning union is the Sanskrit counterpart of the Kural’s earth-and-water couple.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very famous verse; a strong match on inseparable union, though it does not mention sulking or heaven.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
christianity.explanation: Genesis, as Jesus repeats it, describes marriage as two becoming one.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s couple, blended like earth and water, are ‘one flesh’ in just this sense, which is why their quarrel is safe.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on union, but the comparison with heaven and the sulking are absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pictures husband and wife as garments to each other, giving closeness, comfort and covering.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s water soaked into earth, the garment image describes spouses who are wrapped into one another.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih; one sentence excerpted from a longer verse); a good image of intimate union, without the Kural’s comparison to heaven.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that when a man and a woman are worthy, the Divine Presence dwells between them, but when they are not, fire consumes them.
judaism.explanation: A loving marriage is itself a dwelling place for God’s presence.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says no heaven surpasses a loving couple’s bond; the Talmud says such a bond brings heaven down between them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known teaching; a good match on marital union as heavenly, though it says nothing about sulking.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the Buddha’s half-brother Nanda pined for the beautiful Sakyan girl he had left behind, the Buddha took him to a heaven to see celestial nymphs, and Nanda admitted that beside them his earthly beloved looked like a burnt monkey.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses heavenly beauty to loosen Nanda’s attachment, as a step toward letting go of desire altogether.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural reverses this: for its lover, no heavenly world could outshine the joy of a quarrel with the one he loves.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical story; an honest contrast, since the Buddhist text ranks heaven above earthly love (and both below release).

jainism.quote_or_event: “After having enjoyed, in the company of the beautiful ladies of his seraglio, excellent pleasures which match those of the heavens, king Nami became enlightened and gave up his pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain text grants that household love can feel heavenly, then holds up giving it up as the higher path.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural ranks a lover’s quarrel above heaven, while Jain scripture sets even heaven-like pleasures aside for liberation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; shares the comparison of love’s pleasure with heaven, but as a contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves- a few alone reach the land, and these, covered with brine, are thankful when they find themselves on firm ground and out of danger- even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him, and she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Penelope’s long testing of Odysseus ends, Homer compares their reunion to swimmers reaching land after shipwreck.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer’s sea reaching land, after a reunion delayed by the wife’s caution, echoes the Kural’s water joined with earth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu (Butler’s dash kept); a vivid land-and-water image of union, though without the Kural’s comparison to heaven.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes says that human beings were once whole and were split in two, and that love is the desire and pursuit of that lost wholeness, so lovers long to be fused into one.
philosophy.explanation: The myth explains love as the longing of two halves to become one being again.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s lovers, blended like earth and water, have found that wholeness, so even a quarrel between them is joy.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 189c-193d, speech of Aristophanes (tr. Benjamin Jowett; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a strong match on two lovers made one, but the sulking and the comparison with heaven are absent.

kurals.tamil:
புல்லி விடாஅப் புலவியுள் தோன்றுமென்
உள்ளம் உடைக்கும் படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pulli vidaaap pulaviyul thondrumen
Ullam udaikkum padai.
kurals.meaning: Within the sulk that ends in an embrace that will not let go, there appears a weapon that breaks down my resolve.
kurals.elementary: Imagine deciding to stay cross with your best friend all afternoon, and then they do something so sweet that your crossness just melts. Their kindness is like a magic key that unlocks your grumpy mood. The wife says her husband has that kind of key.
kurals.university: The couplet describes a pulavi (‘sulk’) that leads to pulli viṭā (‘embracing and not letting go’, the long vowel in viṭāa marking aḷapeṭai lengthening for metre), within which there arises a paṭai (‘weapon, army’) that uṭaikkum (‘shatters’) eṉ uḷḷam (‘my heart, my firmness’). Commentators identify the weapon with the husband’s tender pleading or caresses, which break the wife’s resolve to keep sulking; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar gloss uḷḷam as uṟuti (‘firmness, determination’). Pope’s ‘a weapon lurks, which quite breaks down my mind’ follows the same line. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the tenth song of the Gita Govinda, Krishna pleads with the sulking Radha, begging her to place her tender foot on his head as an ornament, and her pride begins to melt.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem makes Krishna’s humble pleading the force that overcomes Radha’s māna (proud sulk).
hinduism.tie_back: The lover’s pleading is the ‘weapon’ that, in the Kural too, breaks the sulking partner’s firmness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; a strong thematic fit on pleading that dissolves a beloved’s sulk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me: thy hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Gilead.”
christianity.explanation: The lover in the Song of Songs confesses that the beloved’s gaze has overpowered him.
christianity.tie_back: The beloved’s eyes are the same kind of weapon the Kural names, one that breaks down the will of the one who sees them.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close match on love as an overpowering force, though not set within a sulk.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that a believing man should not hate a believing woman: if he dislikes one of her traits, he will be pleased with another.
islam.explanation: Affection is meant to outweigh passing irritation between spouses.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural, too, irritation gives way because something lovable in the other overcomes it.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; it shares the idea of love outweighing irritation, but not the image of a resolve-breaking weapon.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Scarce had I passed from them, When I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, Until I had brought him into my mother’s house, And into the chamber of her that conceived me.”
judaism.explanation: After searching the city for her beloved, the woman of the Song of Songs finds him and holds on.
judaism.tie_back: ‘I held him, and would not let him go’ is almost the Kural’s pulli viṭā, the embrace that will not let go.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a near match on the clinging embrace, though the resolve-breaking weapon is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Mara’s three daughters, Craving, Discontent and Passion, try every kind of charm on the newly awakened Buddha, but he remains unmoved and they leave defeated.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows a mind so free that even the strongest charms cannot shake it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife freely admits the opposite: love’s weapon breaks her resolve, which is exactly the hold the Buddha escapes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical episode; offered as an honest contrast, since Buddhism prizes the resolve the Kural happily loses.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The five senses, anger, pride, delusion, and greed --difficult to conquer is one’s self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
jainism.explanation: King Nami teaches that self-conquest is the hardest and greatest victory.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is conquered by love’s weapon, the reverse of the Jain ideal of a self that cannot be overcome.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on archive.sacred-texts.com (Jacobi’s page-break dash kept); offered as a contrast between a resolve lost to love and self-mastery.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “As she spoke she loosed from her bosom the curiously embroidered girdle into which all her charms had been wrought- love, desire, and that sweet flattery which steals the judgement even of the most prudent.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Aphrodite lends Hera the girdle whose charms can overpower even Zeus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer’s girdle that ‘steals the judgement’ is the Kural’s weapon that breaks the heart’s firmness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong match on love as a judgement-breaking weapon, though used as a deception.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal wrote that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: Pascal holds that the heart moves by its own logic, which reasoning cannot control.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s reasoned decision to keep sulking is undone by her heart, as Pascal would expect.
philosophy.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées 277 (tr. W. F. Trotter; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line (numbering from the Brunschvicg/Trotter order); a reasonable fit on the heart overriding resolve, though Pascal mainly means knowledge of God.

kurals.tamil:
தவறிலர் ஆயினும் தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள்
அகறலின் ஆங்கொன் றுடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Thavarilar aayinum thaamveezhvaar mendroal
Akaralin aangon rudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: Even when a man has done no wrong, being kept for a while from the tender arms of the woman he loves holds a pleasure of its own.
kurals.elementary: Waiting for a birthday makes the party feel even better when it comes. A husband who is told ‘not now’ by his wife in a playful sulk, even though he did nothing wrong, finds a funny kind of sweetness in the waiting.
kurals.university: Here the voice shifts to the husband, or to a general maxim about men: taviṟilar āyiṉum (‘though they are without fault’), being separated from (akaṟal) the mel tōḷ (‘soft shoulders’, a standard metonymy for the beloved’s embrace) of those whom they love (tām vīḻvār) has āṅku oṉṟu (‘a certain something there’, i.e. a special pleasure). Solomon Pappaiah reads the husband as accepting the role of the guilty one in order to be sulked at, while Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan simply note that such separation contains a pleasure; Pope renders the thought as estrangement having ‘its own special charms’. The couplet is the same on both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the elided form āṅkoṉṟuṭaittu is split as āṅku oṉṟu uṭaittu.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Harivamsa, when Krishna gives a celestial parijata flower to Rukmini, Satyabhama withdraws in a jealous sulk; Krishna, though he meant no slight, patiently soothes her and promises to bring her the whole parijata tree from Indra’s heaven.
hinduism.explanation: The episode became a favourite theme in Indian art and drama for a faultless husband humbly winning back a sulking wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s husband, Krishna is innocent, kept at a distance by his wife’s pique, and finds the wooing worth it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode whose details vary between the Harivamsa, Vishnu Purana and later retellings; a good thematic match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.”
christianity.explanation: In the Song of Songs the beloved stands knocking at night, kept waiting outside the door though he has done nothing wrong.
christianity.tie_back: He is the Kural’s faultless lover, kept for a while from his beloved, with the waiting adding to the longing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a good match on the innocent lover kept waiting, though the Song does not call the delay pleasant.

islam.quote_or_event: “There was something between us and he got angry with me and went out. He did not sleep (midday nap) in the house.” … Allah’s Messenger started cleaning the dust from him saying: “Get up! O Aba Turab. Get up! O Aba Turab”
islam.explanation: After a small quarrel with Fatima, Ali went to sleep in the mosque; the Prophet found him covered in dust and affectionately nicknamed him ‘Father of Dust’.
islam.tie_back: A brief separation after a small domestic quarrel ends in tenderness, close to the Kural’s pleasant estrangement.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (ellipsis marks omitted narrative); a real, affectionate domestic quarrel, though here it is the husband who withdraws.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes says that holding close and holding back each have their proper season.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband discovers that the time of refraining from embrace has its own pleasure.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a good match on embracing and refraining in turn, though it is a general reflection on time.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhallatiya Jataka, a pair of kinnaras (forest spirits) are still weeping, hundreds of years later, over a single night when a flooded stream kept them apart, and they say they have never forgotten it.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows how much a single separation weighs on a loving couple, and the king who hears it learns to value his queen.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband feels the same separation more lightly, as a short absence whose ache sweetens the reunion.
buddhism.source: Jataka 504, Bhallatiya-Jataka (ed. E. B. Cowell; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical Jataka; shares the faultless separation of lovers, but treats it as grief, not pleasure.

jainism.quote_or_event: The monk Sthulabhadra spent a rainy season in the house of Kosha, the courtesan he had once loved, and remained unmoved by every attempt to win him back; his self-control so impressed her that she became a devout laywoman.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative presents a former lover’s nearness, resisted, as a triumph of restraint.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband also stays apart from his beloved’s arms, but he relishes the distance as part of love, which is the opposite of Sthulabhadra’s aim.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous Jain story; a contrast only, since the separation is renunciation, not lovers’ play.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “My dear,” said he, “heaven has endowed you with a heart more unyielding than woman ever yet had. No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he had come back to her after twenty years of absence, and after having gone through so much.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, home at last and blameless towards Penelope, is kept at a distance while she tests him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s faultless husband, Odysseus is held back from his wife’s embrace for a time before the joyful reunion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a good match on a blameless husband kept at a distance, though Odysseus is frustrated rather than pleased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observed that absence lessens moderate passions and increases great ones, as the wind blows out candles but fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: Distance tests love: weak love dies of it, strong love grows.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband feels a strong love grow during a short separation, which is why the separation has its own sweetness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim, not re-checked against the Gutenberg text in this session; a good fit on absence feeding strong love.

kurals.tamil:
உணலினும் உண்டது அறல்இனிது காமம்
புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Unalinum undadhu aral-inidhu kaamam
Punardhalin oodal inidhu.
kurals.meaning: Digesting what one has eaten is sweeter than eating; in love, the sulk is sweeter than being together.
kurals.elementary: After a big lunch, the cosy, full feeling afterwards can feel even nicer than the eating. The poet says love is similar: the little pause of a pretend quarrel can be sweeter than simply being together.
kurals.university: A striking analogy from the body: uṇaliṉum (‘more than eating’) uṇṭatu aṟal (‘the digesting of what has been eaten’, aṟal from aṟu, to be consumed or settle) is iṉitu (‘sweet, pleasant’); likewise in kāmam (love), ūṭal is sweeter than puṇartal (union). Commentators read the parallel as saying that, just as digestion readies one for the next meal, ūṭal renews the appetite of love; Puliyur Kesikan speaks of the pleasure gained ‘by sulking’ exceeding that gained ‘by uniting’. Kalaignar and Pope keep the comparison directly. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh hyphenates aṟal-iṉitu in its transliteration.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Natyashastra divides the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra rasa) into two kinds, love in union (sambhoga) and love in separation (vipralambha), and treats both as full forms of the same sentiment.
hinduism.explanation: Indian poetics gives the longing of a quarrel or separation a full place in the aesthetics of love, not merely a lack of union.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural goes one step further and ranks the separation of a sulk above union itself.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the standard twofold division of śṛṅgāra; a solid theoretical parallel, though the Natyashastra does not rank one above the other.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews says that what is unpleasant at the time brings sweetness afterwards.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s digestion after a meal, the sweetness comes after, not during, the experience.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the shape of a later sweetness, but concerns discipline, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi’s Masnavi opens with the reed flute lamenting that it was cut from its reed-bed, and saying that whoever is parted from his source longs to return to the time of union.
islam.explanation: For Rumi, separation is what gives love its voice and its sweetness of longing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly finds in a short separation a sweetness that union alone does not give.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi I.1-4 (tr. R. A. Nicholson; paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the famous Song of the Reed; a good match on separation deepening love, though Rumi’s longing is mystical.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The full soul loatheth a honeycomb; But to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that sweetness depends on appetite: the full refuse honey, while the hungry relish even bitter food.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same food logic: a pause in love restores the appetite that makes love sweet.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match on appetite and sweetness, though not applied to love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada warns that a person who is sluggish and gluttonous, sleeping and rolling about like a hog fed on grain, keeps returning to birth again and again.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching counsels moderation in eating and in all the pleasures of the senses.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural uses eating and digesting to praise the rhythm of love’s pleasures; the Buddhist verse uses food to warn against indulgence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; an honest contrast that shares only the food imagery.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain text says a pleasure that is sweet in the eating turns to poison in the digesting.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural and the Jain verse use the same eating-and-digestion contrast, but the Kural finds the digesting sweet while the Jain sutra finds it deadly.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; a striking structural parallel used as a contrast, since its verdict on pleasure is the reverse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the limb-loosener and a ‘sweetbitter’ (glukupikron) creature that cannot be resisted.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek love poetry names the mixture of sweetness and pain at the heart of desire.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s sulk is just such a bittersweet ingredient, and it says this makes love sweeter than union alone.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment; a good match on bittersweet love, though Sappho does not compare quarrel and union.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus wrote that although every pleasure is good, not every pleasure is to be chosen, and that we often prefer pains when enduring them for a while brings a greater pleasure afterwards.
philosophy.explanation: Epicurus calculates pleasures over time rather than moment by moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same calculation: the brief pain of a sulk is worth it for the greater sweetness that follows.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 129 (tr. R. D. Hicks; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong fit on choosing a short pain for a greater pleasure, though not about love.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார் அதுமன்னும்
கூடலிற் காணப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodalil thotravar vendraar adhumannum
Kootalir kaanap padum.
kurals.meaning: In a lovers’ quarrel, the one who gives in first is the one who wins, and that is plain to see when they are together again.
kurals.elementary: When two friends argue about who gets the swing first, the one who says ‘you go first’ often ends up having the most fun, because the friendship is happy again. In love, the poet says, whoever gives in first is the real winner.
kurals.university: The paradox ūṭalil tōṟṟavar veṉṟār (‘those who lost in the sulk have won’) is confirmed, the poet says, in kūṭal (reunion), where atu maṉṉum kāṇappaṭum (‘it will surely be seen’; maṉṉum here an emphatic particle). Kalaignar glosses ūṭal as ‘a sweet war’ (iṉiya pōr), and Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan agree that the truth of the paradox is seen when the couple are reconciled. Commentators differ on who ‘loses’: some take it as the partner who yields to the other’s pleading, others as the one who gives up sulking first; the couplet is often quoted on its own as a maxim for marriage. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Kumarasambhava, after Parvati’s long austerities, Shiva reveals himself and tells her that from that day on he is her slave, bought by her penance.
hinduism.explanation: The great ascetic god gives in completely to the woman who has sought him, and their union follows.
hinduism.tie_back: Shiva’s surrender is a divine case of the Kural’s paradox: the one who yields in love wins the beloved.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a celebrated verse; a good match on loving surrender that wins union, though it follows penance rather than a sulk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that lowering oneself is the way to being raised up.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the same reversal to love: whoever lowers himself in the quarrel is the one who wins.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong structural match on the humble being raised, though about pride in general.

islam.quote_or_event: Aisha recalled that she once raced the Prophet on a journey and won; years later, when she had grown heavier, they raced again and he won, and he laughed and said, ‘This is for that.’
islam.explanation: The hadith shows a playful contest between spouses in which winning and losing are both part of their affection.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural’s ‘sweet war’, the real winner of such playful contests is the love between them.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, not re-read in this session; a fair parallel on playful competition between spouses, not on yielding in a quarrel.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud advises that if your wife is short, you should bend down and whisper to her, meaning that a husband should lower himself to consult and listen to his wife.
judaism.explanation: The sages praise a husband who stoops to meet his wife rather than standing over her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s winner is likewise the one willing to bend in the quarrel.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known saying; shares the virtue of yielding to one’s spouse, though not set in a lovers’ quarrel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Victory begets enmity; the defeated dwell in pain. Happily the peaceful live, discarding both victory and defeat.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that winning breeds resentment, and that peace comes from leaving the whole contest behind.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s lovers find the same peace when one of them lays down the contest and lets the other ‘win’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a good match on giving up the win-lose contest, though the Buddhist peace is wider than lovers’ reunion.

jainism.quote_or_event: After defeating his brother Bharata, Bahubali renounced the world and stood in meditation for a year, but his pride kept him from omniscience; when his sisters Brahmi and Sundari told him to come down from the elephant of pride, he humbled himself and at that moment attained kevala jñāna.
jainism.explanation: In Jain tradition, letting go of pride (māna) is what finally brings victory.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s paradox, that the one who gives in wins, matches Bahubali’s story, where yielding pride brings the highest victory.
jainism.source: Hemachandra, Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra, Book 1 (tr. Helen M. Johnson; paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely told Jain story (versions differ in detail); a good structural match, though the setting is spiritual, not romantic.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “When she heard the sure proofs Ulysses now gave her, she fairly broke down. She flew weeping to his side, flung her arms about his neck, and kissed him. ‘Do not be angry with me Ulysses,’ she cried, ‘you, who are the wisest of mankind.’”
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope ends her long resistance and gives way to Odysseus, and husband and wife are reunited.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope ‘loses’ the contest of wills and wins her husband back, as the Kural says the yielding partner does.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu (inner quotation marks made single); a good narrative match on yielding that ends in reunion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Tao Te Ching teaches that what bends is preserved whole and what yields is made straight, and that because the sage does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.
philosophy.explanation: Daoism holds that yielding and not contending lead to the surest victory.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s lover wins by not contending; the Daoist sage does the same.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; a strong structural fit on winning by yielding, though not about lovers.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடிப் பெறுகுவம் கொல்லோ நுதல்வெயர்ப்பக்
கூடலில் தோன்றிய உப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ootip perukuvam kolloa nudhalveyarppak
Kootalil thoandriya uppu.
kurals.meaning: Shall we once more, through a little sulking, win back that sweetness of reunion we knew before?
kurals.elementary: After a really happy day at the beach, you might wish you could have that same day again. The husband in this poem remembers how happy they were after their last make-up, and wonders whether another small quarrel might bring that happiness back.
kurals.university: The husband wonders whether, by sulking again (ūṭi), they will once more peṟukuvam (‘obtain’, first person plural, with the doubting particle kollō) the uppu (literally ‘salt’, figuratively ‘savour, relish’) that arose in kūṭal (reunion), when nutal veyarppa (‘the brow grew moist’). Parimelazhagar and the modern glossators take uppu as the relish or sweetness of love, the salt being the zest that makes food tasty; Mu. Varadarasanar renders it as iṉimai (sweetness). Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss (‘ivaḷuṭaṉ’, with her) confirms the traditional reading of this couplet as the husband’s words. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; thirukkural.net keeps the older spelling veyarppa for viyarppa.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, the exiled yaksha asks a passing cloud to carry a message to his wife, recalling intimate moments of their life together and promising that their love, made deeper by separation, will be enjoyed again when the curse ends.
hinduism.explanation: The poem turns memory of past happiness into hope of its return.
hinduism.tie_back: The yaksha, like the Kural’s husband, remembers a past sweetness and longs to taste it once more.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s closing movement; a fair match on longing to relive past joy, though the separation is a curse, not a sulk.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Draw me, we will run after thee: the king hath brought me into his chambers: we will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs treats love as something to be remembered and savoured, better than wine.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband also remembers love’s savour and longs to taste it again.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the savouring of remembered love, but not the idea of renewing it through a quarrel.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an names among God’s signs that He created spouses for people so that they may find rest in them, and placed between them affection and mercy.
islam.explanation: Marital affection is presented as a gift renewed between spouses.
islam.tie_back: The tender reunion the Kural’s husband hopes to taste again is this kind of affection and mercy.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse (not re-read in this session, so not quoted); a general match on marital affection, not on renewed reunion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Enjoy life with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which He hath given thee under the sun, all the days of thy vanity; for that is thy portion in life, and in thy labour wherein thou labourest under the sun.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes counts the joy of life with a beloved wife as one of the few lasting goods.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband wants to keep tasting that joy, even by means of a playful quarrel.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a general match on enjoying married love, not on renewing it through a sulk.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada teaches that from craving springs grief and from craving springs fear, and that for one free of craving there is neither grief nor fear.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist teaching sees the wish to repeat a pleasure as craving (taṇhā), a root of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband openly hopes to repeat a pleasure, which is just the craving the Dhammapada warns against.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse; an honest contrast, since Buddhism treats the longing to repeat pleasure as a cause of suffering.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain text teaches that sense pleasures never satisfy, so the desire for them only renews itself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wish to taste a pleasure once more is what Jain teaching calls desire that is never satisfied.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com (‘colours’ is Jacobi’s term for all visible objects); an honest contrast on wanting pleasure again.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “As soon as he did so he became inflamed with the same passionate desire for her that he had felt when they had first enjoyed each other’s embraces, and slept with one another without their dear parents knowing anything about it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Zeus sees Hera, his love returns as strong as it was at the start of their romance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s husband hopes for the same thing, that an old sweetness can return as fresh as the first time.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a fair match on remembered first love returning, though in a scene of divine trickery.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Repetition, Kierkegaard’s pseudonym Constantin Constantius tests whether a past joy can be lived again by returning to the place where he once enjoyed it, and contrasts the backward longing of recollection with the forward hope of repetition.
philosophy.explanation: Kierkegaard asks whether lost happiness can be truly repeated rather than merely remembered.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband asks the same question of love: whether another sulk can give back that earlier sweetness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the book’s central question; a good philosophical match on whether joy can be repeated, though Kierkegaard’s answer is complex.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடுக மன்னோ ஒளியிழை யாமிரப்ப
நீடுக மன்னோ இரா.
kurals.transliteration:
Ootuka mannoa oliyizhai yaamirappa
Needuka mannoa iraa.
kurals.meaning: Let her with the shining jewels sulk a little longer, and let the night grow longer too, so that I may go on pleading with her.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes making up with a friend is so much fun that you almost wish the game would go on. Here a husband enjoys coaxing his wife out of her playful sulk so much that he wishes the night would stretch out, so he can keep coaxing.
kurals.university: Both lines turn on the optative with the particle maṉṉō (‘O, may it be so!’): ūṭuka (‘may she sulk’) and nīṭuka (‘may it lengthen’), framing the hero’s wish. Oḷi iḻai (‘she of bright jewels’) is a standard epithet for the heroine, and yām irappa (‘so that I may beg, plead’) gives the reason for wanting the night (irā) to stretch on. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan agree in reading the couplet as the husband’s wish that her sulk and the night both continue so that he may keep entreating her; Pope renders it ‘That I may still plead on, O night, prolong thy reign!’ The text is the same on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Bhagavata Purana says that on the night of the Rasa dance Krishna extended the night so that it lasted as long as a night of Brahma, and the gopis enjoyed his company throughout it.
hinduism.explanation: The divine lover stretches time itself so that the night of love will not end.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband wishes for exactly this, a night prolonged so that the play of love can continue.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse in the Rasa-lila; a close match on a night prolonged for love, in a devotional setting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a friend knocking at midnight is answered because he keeps on asking.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband, too, keeps on pleading through the night, and enjoys the asking.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a next-best match on persistent pleading at night, set in prayer rather than love.

islam.quote_or_event: In the hadith of Umm Zar‘, Aisha tells the Prophet a long story of eleven women describing their husbands; he listens to the end and then tells her that he is to her as Abu Zar‘, the kindest husband in the tale, was to Umm Zar‘.
islam.explanation: The hadith shows the Prophet patiently enjoying his wife’s company and conversation.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s husband, who wants the night to last, the Prophet takes pleasure in lingering time with his wife.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5189, hadith of Umm Zar‘ (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; it shows loving, unhurried time together, but has no sulk or prolonged night.

judaism.quote_or_event: In the Book of Ruth, Ruth comes to Boaz at night on the threshing floor and asks him to take her under his protection; he tells her to stay the night until morning, and promises to act on her request.
judaism.explanation: The scene is one of the Bible’s tenderest night encounters, full of courteous asking and answering.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a night of gentle pleading leads to a loving union.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a next-best match on a night of pleading between future spouses, without any sulk or wish for a longer night.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kusa Jataka, the Bodhisatta as King Kusa, whose wife Pabhavati has left him, follows her to her father’s city and humbly works as a potter, basket-maker, gardener and cook, trying again and again to win her back until at last she returns to him.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka is a story of a lover’s long, humble persistence in pleading.
buddhism.tie_back: Kusa’s patient pleading resembles the Kural’s husband, who is happy to keep pleading with his sulking wife.
buddhism.source: Jataka 531, Kusa Jataka (ed. E. B. Cowell; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical Jataka; a fair match on persistent wooing of an estranged wife, though her estrangement is real rather than playful.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Tamil Jain epic Jivaka Chintamani follows its hero through a series of romances and marriages, celebrated at length in courtly love poetry, before he finally renounces the world and becomes a Jain monk.
jainism.explanation: The epic gives full poetic space to married love, while framing it as a stage that ends in renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Its love poetry shares the Kural’s delight in lovers’ time together, but its ending places that delight below renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of the epic’s arc (a Tamil Jain text); a weak, next-best match, since no specific scene of a prolonged night of pleading is cited.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Indeed they would have gone on indulging their sorrow till rosy-fingered morn appeared, had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west, while she would not suffer Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to yoke the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind.”
greek_mythology.explanation: On the night Odysseus and Penelope are reunited, Athena holds back the dawn to lengthen their night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s husband prays for the very thing Athena grants the reunited couple, a longer night.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a near match on a night lengthened for a reconciled couple, though here a goddess acts rather than a lover wishing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Amores 1.13, Ovid scolds Dawn for coming too soon and taking him from his beloved, and begs the horses of Night to run slowly (lente currite, noctis equi), a line Marlowe later borrowed for Doctor Faustus.
philosophy.explanation: Roman love poetry has a whole genre of the lover’s complaint against the dawn.
philosophy.tie_back: Ovid’s plea to slow the horses of Night is the Kural’s nīṭuka maṉṉō irā, ‘may the night be long’.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known elegy (a Roman poet, used here in the philosophy slot as in earlier chapters); a close match on wishing the night prolonged.

kurals.tamil:
ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம் அதற்கின்பம்
கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodudhal kaamaththirku inpam adharkinpam
Kooti muyangap perin.
kurals.meaning: Sulking is the delight of love, and the delight of sulking is to make up and be held close again.
kurals.elementary: A pretend quarrel is a little game that makes love fun, and the best part of the game is the big hug when it is over. With this happy thought, the whole Thirukkural comes to an end.
kurals.university: The last couplet of the Kural is built as a chain: ūṭutal kāmattiṟku iṉpam (‘sulking is a delight to love’), ataṟku iṉpam (‘its delight in turn’) is kūṭi muyaṅkap peṟiṉ (‘if one gets to come together and embrace’, muyaṅku meaning to clasp). Solomon Pappaiah adds that the embrace should come aḷavu aṟintu (‘knowing the right measure’), i.e. the sulk must not be stretched too far, a point Parimelazhagar’s tradition also stresses, and Mu. Varadarasanar reads the embrace as the delight that crowns the sulk. Pope ends his translation with ‘The pleasure’s crowned when breast is clasped to breast.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; with this couplet both the kaṟpiyal and the whole 1,330-couplet work conclude, on a note of reconciled love.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita Govinda ends with Radha and Krishna reunited after her long sulk; Radha, now at ease, playfully asks Krishna to adorn her and rearrange her ornaments, and he gladly obeys.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem completes the cycle of separation, sulking and reconciliation with a tender, playful reunion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s last couplet, the Gita Govinda ends with the sulk resolved in loving closeness.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s final canto; a strong match on a reconciliation that crowns the sulk, kept tasteful here.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows spouses to stay apart only for a short, agreed time, and then tells them to come together again.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s cycle is similar: a short separation whose proper end is coming together again.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV; quotation stops before the verse ends); shares the separation-then-reunion pattern, though for prayer rather than play.

islam.quote_or_event: Ibn Hazm’s Ring of the Dove, a classic Andalusian treatise on love, devotes chapters to reproach between lovers and to union, treating gentle reproach as part of love and reunion as its sweetest moment.
islam.explanation: Classical Arabic love literature sees lovers’ reproach and reconciliation as a natural rhythm of love.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s last word, that the joy of a sulk is the reunion, fits the same courtly understanding of love.
islam.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (tr. A. J. Arberry; paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: General paraphrase of the treatise’s chapters on reproach and union, not checked against a live text; a cultural rather than scriptural Islamic source.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His left hand should be under my head, And his right hand should embrace me.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs repeats this longing for the beloved’s embrace near its close.
judaism.tie_back: The embrace is the crown of the Kural’s sulk, as it is the woman’s wish in the Song.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a good match on the longed-for embrace, though there is no quarrel before it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nakulapita and Nakulamata tell the Buddha that since their marriage in youth neither has ever been unfaithful even in thought, and that they wish to see each other in this life and in lives to come; the Buddha tells them how a couple may stay together in future lives.
buddhism.explanation: The Samajivina Sutta honours a married couple whose love has lasted a lifetime.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural ends with lovers reunited after a quarrel; the Buddha’s model couple shows such reunion lasting a whole life and beyond.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical sutta; a fair match on enduring married love, though it says nothing about lovers’ quarrels.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain text teaches that love and anger both arise from attachment, and that freedom lies in going beyond both.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural celebrates the turn from anger (the sulk) to love (the embrace); Jainism sees both as two faces of the same attachment.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; an honest contrast, since Jain teaching seeks freedom from both sulk and embrace.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Apuleius’ tale, after Psyche loses Cupid through her own doubt and endures many trials, the lovers are at last reunited, Psyche is made immortal, and their wedding is celebrated among the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story of Cupid and Psyche moves from estrangement through suffering to a lasting, joyful union.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s final couplet, the tale ends with separation crowned by loving reunion.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known tale (Latin, on a Greek mythic theme); its estrangement is serious rather than playful.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal describes how, once love is established, a moment of doubt about the beloved gives rise to a second ‘crystallization’, in which love, reassured, becomes stronger than before.
philosophy.explanation: In Stendhal’s analysis, a passing doubt deepens love once it is resolved.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s cycle of sulk and embrace follows the same pattern: a short uncertainty, then a stronger, sweeter love.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love (De l’amour, 1822), Book 1, chs. 2-3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Stendhal’s well-known theory; a reasonable fit on doubt resolved into deeper love, though his doubt is not a playful sulk.
